stem: Salts which can be used as supplement of calcium and iron are obtained from -------- acid.
note: Two printed oddities, neither answer-affecting. (1) The blank is followed by the word 'acid', while the option list offers the full phrase 'gluconic acid' - so the word actually required in the blank is 'gluconic'. (2) The chapter table this answer comes from (printed p81) is headed 'Amino acid' over a column containing citric, gluconic, lactic and itaconic acid, none of which is an amino acid; the table's own title calls them 'Organic acids used in various commercial products'. The heading is wrong, the row is right.

Match the pairs.

| 'A' group | 'B' group |
|---|---|
| a. Xylitol | 1. Pigment |
| b. Citric acid | 2. To impart sweetness |
| c. Lycopene | 3. Microbial restrictor |
| d. Nycin | 4. Protein binding emulsifier |
|  | 5. To impart acidity |
note: The 'B' group prints FIVE roles against FOUR items in the 'A' group, so one role is a deliberate distractor. Item 4 'Protein binding emulsifier' fuses two separate rows of the chapter's own table (printed p81), which lists 'Protein binding' (glutamic acid, lysine, tryptophan) and 'Emulsifiers' (polysaccharides, glycolipids) as distinct roles. The book spells the antimicrobial peptide 'Nycin' both here and in that table; it is internally consistent, so the printed spelling is kept.

What are the benefits of mixing ethanol with petrol and diesel?
note: NOT ANSWERABLE FROM THIS CHAPTER. The words 'petrol' and 'diesel' occur nowhere in the chapter except in this question, and the chapter never mentions blending ethanol into any fuel. All it supplies is that ethanol is a clean (smokeless) fuel obtained by fermentation of molasses by Saccharomyces, and that biofuels are renewable and reliable fuels of the future. The stored answer says so explicitly rather than importing the standard outside-knowledge list of blending benefits.

stem: Which plants are cultivated to obtain the fuel?
note: NOT ANSWERABLE AS ASKED FROM THIS CHAPTER. The chapter names NO plant species anywhere in connection with fuel - 'cultivated' occurs only in this question, and fig. 7.8 draws the biomass stage as unlabelled generic trees. The chapter names only plant-derived RAW MATERIALS (sugar molasses, starch of the roots, fruit juices, maple syrup, crop residue, vegetable oils, cellulose). The stored answer gives those and states plainly that the chapter names no fuel crop.
